reference.text: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., CRC Press, 2013, chapters 1–2.
content.0: Imagine pulling a coin from a magic drawer. You don’t know its probability of landing heads, but you initially think it is probably close to 50%.
content.1: Bayesian inference combines what we knew before collecting data with what the new data tell us. A prior distribution represents uncertainty about an unknown parameter before observing the data; the posterior distribution represents uncertainty after the data are observed.

content.9: You start flipping it. If you see lots of heads, you begin to think the probability of heads may be higher than 50%. If you then see more tails, your belief may shift back down.
content.10: This is Bayesian updating: start with a belief, observe new evidence, and use that evidence to update your belief. Even after several flips, you can still be uncertain about the coin’s true bias.
